nameStory: The "inchplant" gets its name from how quickly it grows - you can practically watch it creep along inch by inch! It's also called "wandering dude" because of its trailing, wandering growth habit as it spreads across the ground or spills from hanging baskets. The "zebrina" part of its scientific name refers to the zebra-like silver and green stripes on its leaves.
description: Inchplant is a trailing, creeping plant with eye-catching striped leaves that's become a popular houseplant. In New England's climate, you'll mostly find it as an indoor plant or occasionally escaped from cultivation in protected spots. The plant has a cascading growth habit, sending out long trailing stems that root wherever they touch soil. Its most distinctive feature is its silvery-green striped foliage that gives it an almost metallic shimmer.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves with distinctive silver and green zebra stripes running lengthwise, feeling slightly succulent and smooth to the touch with a glossy surface that catches light

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Long trailing stems that creep along the ground or cascade from containers, easily rooting at joints where they touch soil

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Purple-tinged stems that feel somewhat fleshy and break easily, with visible joints or nodes every few inches

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small three-petaled purple or pink flowers that appear sporadically, though flowering is uncommon on houseplants

idTips.label: Leaf Arrangement
idTips.description: Leaves alternate along the stem and clasp around it at the base, creating a neat overlapping pattern

habitat: In New England, inchplant is primarily found as a houseplant or in greenhouses, as it cannot survive our winters outdoors. Very rarely, you might find it escaped from cultivation in warm, protected microclimates near buildings or in heavily disturbed areas during summer months. It prefers partial shade and moist, well-draining soil when grown outdoors in warmer climates.

seasonality.spring: Houseplants show most vigorous growth as daylight increases, with new shoots extending rapidly and leaves showing their brightest coloration.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season for potted plants, which may be moved outdoors to shaded porches or patios where they'll trail dramatically from hanging baskets.
seasonality.fall: Growth slows as light decreases; any outdoor plants must be brought inside before first frost or they'll be killed by cold temperatures.
seasonality.winter: Indoor plants continue growing slowly in bright windows, though lower light may cause some loss of the bright silver striping in the leaves.

funFact: This plant is practically indestructible - you can propagate a whole new plant from just a single leaf cutting placed in water, and it will develop roots within days, making it one of the easiest plants to share with friends!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other trailing houseplants, but the distinctive silver zebra striping makes it quite unmistakable once you know what to look for. Remember: if it has metallic-looking stripes and purple stems, you've found inchplant!
contextualKnowledge: This plant was formerly called "wandering Jew," but many people now prefer "wandering dude" or simply "inchplant" as more inclusive alternatives. Be aware that some consider this plant invasive in warmer climates, so it's best kept as a houseplant in New England rather than planted outdoors.
compareHints: Unlike our native Virginia spiderwort with its grass-like leaves and blue flowers, inchplant has broad, striped leaves and rarely flowers indoors. Purple heart (another Tradescantia) has solid purple leaves without stripes, while Ohio spiderwort grows upright rather than trailing. The zebra-striped pattern and creeping habit make inchplant unique among its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Virginia spiderwort is the most common spiderwort in New England and has the classic blue-purple flowers and smooth leaves.
Ohio spiderwort differs from Virginia spiderwort mainly in its hairless sepals and slightly more robust growth habit.

Compared to Virginia spiderwort (the most common spiderwort in New England), longbract spiderwort has much longer bracts extending well beyond the flower clusters, while Ohio spiderwort has hairless leaves (longbract's are slightly hairy).
Unlike its native New England spiderwort cousins like Virginia spiderwort, Purple Heart has distinctly purple foliage year-round rather than green leaves.
